\chapter{Not There, Not So}
\label{ch:ml-alla}
\hlchaptermodality{77}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is not what it was called, and I can check something I think I already know.}

From cold: both negatives and the question each one answers, and the tag built from the second of them.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[alla]{\ml{അല്ല} (alla) — \textquotedblleft{}is not so\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C77-alla}



\begin{quote}
Two words you have had since the opening chapters: the one that says something \textbf{is}, and the one that says something \textbf{is not there}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{അല്ല}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ} \ml{അല്ല}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ñān adhyāpakan alla} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I am not a teacher.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} is the negative of \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}. Where \ml{ആണ്} says \emph{X is Y}, \ml{അല്ല} says \emph{X is not Y} — and it sits in the same place, at the end, where the sentence closes.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Malayalam negates twice, and English only once}]
You now hold \textbf{two} negatives, and they are not interchangeable:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}} & it is \textbf{not there} — denies that something exists \\
\textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} & it is \textbf{not so} — denies that something is what you called it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English spends one word on both. \emph{There is no tea} and \emph{this is not tea} both use \textbf{not}, and Malayalam will not let you.

That is the thing to carry: before you reach for a negative in this language, \textbf{ask which question you are answering.} \emph{Is there any?} takes \ml{ഇല്ല}. \emph{Is it that?} takes \ml{അല്ല}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{alla} — is not so
  \item \emph{ñān adhyāpakan alla}
  \item which negative answers \emph{is there any tea?}
  \item which negative answers \emph{is this tea?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \emph{I am not a teacher}? (\emph{\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ} \ml{അല്ല}}}.) Which word does \ml{അല്ല} negate? (\emph{\textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}}.) And which negative would you use to say something is not present? (\emph{\textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[allē]{\ml{അല്ലേ} (allē) — \textquotedblleft{}isn't it?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C77-alle}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{is not so}. Then say the letter Malayalam adds to turn a statement into a genuine question.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{അല്ലേ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾ} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ} \ml{ആണ്}, \ml{അല്ലേ}?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{niṅṅaḷ adhyāpakan āṇ, allē?} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{You are a teacher, aren't you?}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Look at the front of it. \textbf{\ml{അല്ലേ}} opens on \textbf{\ml{അല്ല}}, the word from the last lesson, and that containment is the whole of why it means what it means: it hangs \emph{\textquotedblleft{}or is it not so?\textquotedblright{}} on the end of a statement you have already made.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: asking, and asking for agreement}]
Malayalam has \textbf{two ways to end a sentence with a question}, and they want different things back:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-\ml{ഓ}} & a genuine question — \emph{I do not know; tell me} \\
\textbf{\ml{അല്ലേ}} & a tag — \emph{I think I know; agree with me} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ml{ചായ} \ml{വേണോ}?} genuinely does not know whether you want tea. \textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾ} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ} \ml{ആണ്}, \ml{അല്ലേ}?} is fairly sure you are one and is checking.

English hides this difference inside intonation and a repeated verb — \emph{you are, aren't you}. Malayalam puts it in one word and does not change the sentence in front of it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{allē?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{niṅṅaḷ adhyāpakan āṇ, allē?}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ml{അല്ലേ}} and find \textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} inside it
  \item \emph{Say it:} which ending you would use if you genuinely did not know
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ml{അല്ലേ}} invite — an answer, or agreement? (\textbf{Agreement}.) Which word is hiding at the front of it? (\emph{\textbf{\ml{അല്ല}}}.) And which ending asks a question you truly do not know the answer to? (\textbf{-\ml{ഓ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[illa alla ōrmma]{(not there, not so) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R77-not-so-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say both negatives, and say which question each one answers.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one English word, two Malayalam ones}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{denies} & \textbf{pairs with} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}} & that it is \textbf{there} & \emph{is there any?} \\
\textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} & that it is \textbf{so} & \emph{is it that?} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{English spends one word where Malayalam spends two}, so the choice is a decision English never made you make. Make it by looking at the question, not at the word you would use at home.

\textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} is the negative of \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}, which is why it closes a sentence in the same place \ml{ആണ്} does.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The ability to say what something \textbf{is not} — and, from that same word, to check something you think you already know.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾ} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ} \ml{ആണ്}, \ml{അല്ലേ}?}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ml{അല്ലേ}} carries \textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} at its front, and hangs \emph{\textquotedblleft{}or is it not so?\textquotedblright{}} on a statement. It invites agreement where \textbf{-\ml{ഓ}} asks for an answer.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ñān adhyāpakan alla}
  \item the same idea as a tag question about somebody else
  \item which negative answers \emph{is there any?}
  \item which negative answers \emph{is it that?}
  \item the difference between what \textbf{-\ml{ഓ}} wants and what \textbf{\ml{അല്ലേ}} wants
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{I am not a teacher}. (\emph{\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ} \ml{അല്ല}}}.) How many negatives does Malayalam have where English has one? (\textbf{Two}.) And what does \textbf{\ml{അല്ലേ}} ask for? (\textbf{Agreement}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
